interest: For historians of modern Japan and international relations, this file provides an extraordinarily detailed, real-time chronicle of the Japanese state's structural transition from semi-parliamentary governance toward an indigenous totalitarian wartime regime. A major highlight is Despatch No. 3081, which preserves a massive 23-page itemized inventory documenting hundreds of specific Japanese military violations, assaults, property seizures, and atrocities against American hospitals, schools, and missions across China—including contemporaneous evidence from Nanking. The collection is equally valuable for its exhaustive primary studies of wartime socioeconomic planning, notably Max W. Schmidt's memorandum on the apparatus of the National General Mobilization Law, as well as rare consular records capturing internal ideological friction, such as Kobe University president Dr. Shinji Tasaki's outspoken public critique of military dominance.
overview: This file documents the domestic political transformations, wartime economic controls, and diplomatic friction in Japan from early 1938 through January 1939 during the escalating Second Sino-Japanese War, prefaced by State Department docket sheets indexing military and naval intelligence from 1930 to 1939. Through extensive diplomatic despatches, confidential telegrams, and analytical memoranda from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and the Tokyo Embassy, the records trace the severe factional divisions within Prince Fumimaro Konoe's Cabinet over continental strategy, the May 1938 ministerial reconstruction incorporating military leaders and business magnate Seihin Ikeda, Foreign Minister Kazushige Ugaki's resignation over the creation of the China Board (Tai Shi In / Koa-in), and the ultimate collapse of the Konoe ministry in favor of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma's authoritarian administration. Interwoven with this political narrative are deep investigations into Japan's total-war mobilization under the National General Mobilization Law—encompassing raw-material import-export controls, labor transfers, and spiritual mobilization campaigns—alongside intensive American diplomatic representations contesting Japanese military violations of the Open Door policy, extraterritorial rights, and widespread destruction of American missionary, commercial, and diplomatic properties in China.
